newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania gypsies fear France immigration clampdown.
newsitem.headline: Romania gypsies fear France immigration clampdown.

text.p: French government efforts to crack down on illegal immigration struck a raw chord among Romanian gypsy leaders as they coincided with a visit to Bucharest by President Jacques Chirac.

"I know how important this visit has been to boost Romania's hopes to join NATO with French support. But I can't help feeling a little bitter," Nicolae Gheorghe, leader of the Roma (Gypsies) Federation, told Reuters.

Gheorghe objects to stricter rules sought by French Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre. In Paris, artists, intellectuals and left-wing opposition parties turned out for marches on Saturday in protest against the draft legislation.
"We are concerned at what is happening in France lately, with police expelling so-called illegal immigrants, especially Gypsies, and sending them back to Romania," Gheorghe said.

During his two-day visit, Chirac has backed Romania's drive for integration into Western structures, and praised the country's new centrist leaders for pledging faster reforms since they ousted ex-communists in elections last November.
But he was much more reserved on the prospects of France dropping visa requirements any time soon for Romanians.
"It (visas) is a delicate problem, which will be solved with the development of Europe," he said during a question-and-answer session with Bucharest University students.
France this month expelled 29 illegal Romanian immigrants, including 10 who had completed jail terms.

It was the 35th chartered flight organised by French authorities, most of which have been bound for Romania and West and Central Africa -- part of Debre's drive to stamp out what he says is the changing nature of illegal immigration.
The extreme right-wing National Front, which took control of its fourth town council last month, demands restrictions on immigrants' rights.

Debre, who accompanied Chirac on his two-day visit to meet Romania's new centrist leaders, signed accords with his Romanian counterpart to tighten police cooperation in fighting illegal immigration, organised crime and terrorism.
"I expect the hard core of those accords to be repatriation of Romanian asylum-seekers in France, or the so-called illegal immigrants, many of whom are Romanian Gypsies," Gheorghe said.

"Romanian citizens seeking asylum in France will be a 'bargaining chip' during Chirac's visit, in exchange for political support," he said of Romania's efforts to muster support for its bid to be among first NATO entrants in July.

Bucharest signed a similar repatriation deal with Bonn in 1992 to discourage the flow of asylum-seekers in search for a better life in the West after the 1989 collapse of communism. Census data show some 400,000 Gypsies live in Romania, but their leaders say the figure is much higher.
